The system automatically analyses village-level planning and spending records — development plans, sanctions, payments, works and photo evidence from Gram Panchayats, blocks, and districts — and surfaces patterns worth an official's attention. The current data is a 20-Gram-Panchayat sample; percentages describe the sample, not the state.

Your readers are busy block-, district- and state-level officials, not data analysts. They read these insights to decide where to direct attention: which districts to question, which records to reconcile, which local practices to check at the next review.

This should be interesting enough to catch a reader's attention and easy enough to understand that the officer doesn't need to read the subsequent paragraph simply to understand it. Lead with what the officer would act on — usually the size and direction of the issue — rather than with the statistical pattern.

DETAIL: <the detail paragraph>
===FINDING 2===
LEAD: ...
DETAIL: ...

...and so on, one block per finding.

response_text:
===FINDING 1===
LEAD: Across the 20-Gram-Panchayat sample, recorded expenditure on 5,630 costed activities was ₹51.96 crore below planned cost. Rangeilunda and Kalimela warrant first attention, with gaps of ₹9.11 crore and ₹5.90 crore respectively.
DETAIL: The shortfall is spread across all 16 sampled blocks and nearly every asset category, rather than being driven by one block or type of work; Banking Facilities was the only category without a clear pattern. Rangeilunda recorded ₹2.73 crore spent against ₹11.84 crore planned and Kalimela ₹1.76 crore against ₹7.65 crore, both about 23% utilisation. At the next review, ask these blocks to reconcile plans, work status and expenditure entries, while checking the broader shortfall across other blocks; the data alone cannot show whether funds remain unspent, works are ongoing, or spending records are incomplete.

===FINDING 1===
LEAD: Recorded spending on costed activities is Rs 51.96 crore below planned cost across the 20-GP sample, and the gap is widespread rather than confined to one block or asset category.
DETAIL: In 27 of the 28 asset-category groupings, the shortfall is distributed across the 16 sampled blocks. Rangeilunda and Kalimela have the largest block-level gaps—Rs 9.11 crore and Rs 5.90 crore—and recorded spending equals only 23.1% and 23.0% of planned cost respectively. Banking Facilities shows no clear distribution pattern. Review the larger gaps to distinguish works not yet due for expenditure from delayed works, incomplete payment records or plans that need closure or revision.

===FINDING 4===
LEAD: For activities with sanctions on file, recorded spending is Rs 5.02 crore below the sanctioned amount across the nine sampled districts; no single district or major asset category explains the gap.
DETAIL: Ganjam has the largest district-level difference, with Rs 4.61 crore spent against Rs 6.30 crore sanctioned, followed by Khordha with Rs 3.33 crore spent against Rs 4.06 crore. The gap is broadly distributed across districts in 27 of 28 asset-category groupings, while Banking Facilities shows no clear pattern. Because only about one in six activities has a sanction record, this is not a programme-wide utilisation rate; review sanction coverage and reconcile older unspent sanctions, particularly in Ganjam and Khordha.

===FINDING 5===
LEAD: Two undocumented output codes account for 92.2% of planned untied funding for public works, making it difficult to see what Rs 51.78 crore is intended to finance.
DETAIL: Code 101 accounts for Rs 34.88 crore and Code 105 for Rs 16.90 crore out of Rs 56.20 crore in planned untied funds. These two codes lead in 19 of the 20 sampled GPs; Haldikudar follows a different pattern. Obtain and apply descriptions for Codes 101–110, then check whether Haldikudar’s coding reflects a genuine planning difference or inconsistent classification.

===FINDING 7===
LEAD: More than half of public works—5,181 of 9,418, or 55.0%—have no asset category recorded, limiting oversight of what the works are creating.
DETAIL: “Uncategorised” is the largest group in 19 of the 20 sampled GPs; Govindapur is the only exception. The next-largest category, Buildings, contains only 688 activities. Ask the 19 GPs to complete or correct asset classification, and review Govindapur’s recording practice to see whether it can be adopted elsewhere.

===FINDING 8===
LEAD: Activities still recorded as “Activity Approved” account for Rs 41.61 crore of the Rs 51.96 crore gap between planned cost and recorded spending.
DETAIL: These activities make up 53.9% of costed activities but show only Rs 14.00 lakh spent against Rs 41.75 crore planned, a utilisation level of 0.3%. This pattern appears in 18 of the 20 sampled GPs; Boipariguda and Laxmipur show no clear pattern. Check whether these are genuinely unstarted approvals, stale status records, future-year plans or missing expenditure entries; also correct the known “Buildings” status mis-coding.

===FINDING 10===
LEAD: Nearly all recorded spending from the General social-category component—Rs 28.59 crore, or 93.9%—is attached to works still marked “WORK ONGOING.”
DETAIL: The pattern holds in 18 of the 20 sampled GPs, while Boipariguda and Laxmipur show no clear pattern. Completed works account for only Rs 23.98 lakh, while Rs 1.15 crore is linked to works marked abandoned. At the next review, reconcile work status with vouchers and physical progress, especially for abandoned works and works that may be complete but remain recorded as ongoing; these figures cover only the General component, not total spending.

===FINDING 12===
LEAD: Almost all recorded expected beneficiaries—2,03,534 people, or 98.4%—are attached to activities still marked “Activity Approved,” while completed works record none.
DETAIL: This pattern appears in 18 of the 20 sampled GPs; Boipariguda and Laxmipur show no clear pattern. Beneficiary information is present for only 763 activities, and the figures are expectations rather than evidence that services were delivered. Review whether status and beneficiary fields are being updated together, particularly for completed and ongoing activities, before using these totals to assess coverage.

===FINDING 13===
LEAD: Half of planned untied funding for costed activities—Rs 30.07 crore, or 50.4%—is directed to Theme 6, “Self-sufficient Infrastructure in Village,” across the 20-GP sample.
DETAIL: Theme 6 receives the largest untied allocation in 18 GPs. Boipariguda is the exception where “Unmapped theme” leads, while Kalimela gives the largest allocation to Theme 4, “Water Sufficient Village.” Review the rationale for these two local patterns and correct missing theme mappings, particularly because unmapped activities account for Rs 5.70 crore of planned untied funding.

===FINDING 14===
LEAD: Code 101 shows a ₹2.49 crore gap between sanctioned and recorded expenditure for new works—by far the largest shortfall among the output types in this 20-GP sample.
DETAIL: Code 101 had ₹14.94 crore spent against ₹17.43 crore sanctioned, or 85.7% utilisation, and recorded the largest absolute shortfall in 19 of the 20 GPs; Chikilli showed no clear pattern. Because sanction records exist for only about one in six activities, this is not a programme-wide utilisation rate; officials should reconcile missing sanctions and payments and establish what the undescribed output codes represent before assessing performance.

===FINDING 15===
LEAD: All 6,893 geotagged photo uploads recorded for new works in this comparison are attached to Code 101, although that code represents only 32.8% of the activities.
DETAIL: Code 101 accounted for most uploads in 19 of the 20 GPs, while Chikilli showed no clear pattern; Codes 102, 103, 109 and 110 had no uploads in these records. Since none of the output codes has a description on file, check whether evidence is being systematically mapped to Code 101, whether other work types lack photo evidence, and whether Chikilli’s records are complete.

===FINDING 17===
LEAD: Codes 101 and 105 have the largest gaps between planned cost and recorded expenditure across every beneficiary-purpose group. Their respective shortfalls are ₹30.97 crore and ₹15.11 crore in this sample.
DETAIL: Code 101 records ₹15.88 crore spent against ₹46.85 crore planned, while Code 105 records ₹7.32 crore against ₹22.43 crore; the same two codes rank lowest for general-public, General, SC and ST activities. This comparison is against planned cost, not sanctioned funds, so it does not by itself prove delayed or unused funding; review implementation and payment status and obtain descriptions for these output codes.

===FINDING 18===
LEAD: Tied funding for costed activities is concentrated almost entirely in sanitation and drinking water: ₹8.82 crore and ₹8.42 crore respectively in this 20-GP sample.
DETAIL: Sanitation accounts for 49.9% and drinking water for 47.7% of the ₹17.66 crore in planned tied funding, and they lead across all four beneficiary-purpose groups. Roads are a distant third at ₹31.01 lakh; the next review should confirm that this concentration reflects the grant conditions and local plans, rather than incomplete or inconsistent focus-area classification.

===FINDING 19===
LEAD: Chikilli has no sanctioned amount recorded in any of the six years, despite accounting for 5.0% of the activities in the sample. This is a clear record-reconciliation priority.
DETAIL: Chikilli is the lowest of the 20 GPs in every year from 2020-21 to 2025-26, with ₹0 sanctioned recorded, while the sample total is ₹28.84 crore. Since sanction data are present for only about one in six activities overall, the records cannot establish that Chikilli received no sanctions; officials should check for missing sanction entries, failed activity linkages or use of another recording process.

===FINDING 21===
LEAD: Spending against “Other” grant components remains the smallest category in every year, at ₹1.02 crore or 3.6% of recorded General-category expenditure.
DETAIL: Of the ₹28.48 crore recorded, ₹16.75 crore was classified as Untied and ₹10.71 crore as Tied, compared with ₹1.02 crore as Other; this ordering holds from 2020-21 through 2025-26. The pattern does not indicate a problem by itself, but officials may wish to identify what is being placed under “Other” and confirm that component codes are consistently classified.

===FINDING 22===
LEAD: Only 17 of 12,704 activities are recorded as completed, while 10,108 remain at “Activity Approved” and 2,110 are marked “WORK ONGOING.” The status register needs an ageing and data-quality review.
DETAIL: The same dominance of approved and ongoing statuses appears in every fiscal year; a further 420 activities are marked abandoned and 36 remain under approval. Officials should identify older approved and ongoing activities, verify whether completed works have not been updated, review the abandoned cases, and correct the 13 records where “Buildings” has been entered as a status.

===FINDING 2===
LEAD: Activity-linked expenditure in the 20-GP sample has risen substantially overall, reaching Rs 5.92 crore in 2025-26 compared with Rs 42.43 lakh in 2020-21. The upward pattern appears at monthly, quarterly and annual levels.
DETAIL: The sample recorded Rs 24.00 crore of activity-linked expenditure across the six years. The rise was not uninterrupted—annual expenditure fell to Rs 3.66 crore in 2023-24 before increasing to Rs 5.06 crore in 2024-25 and Rs 5.92 crore in 2025-26. Reviews should check whether this growth reflects more works, improved linking of payments to planned activities, higher work costs or a combination of these factors.

===FINDING 6===
LEAD: Bhubaneswar accounted for one-quarter of all payment vouchers in the sample and recorded the highest voucher count among blocks in five of the six years. Its unusually high transaction volume merits comparison with its workload and number of GPs covered.
DETAIL: Bhubaneswar recorded 2,135 of the sample’s 8,529 vouchers, well ahead of Rangeilunda at 945 and Bheden at 885. The only exception was 2024-25, when there was no clear block leader; officials should check whether Bhubaneswar’s recurring lead reflects genuine implementation volume, more fragmented payments or differences in cashbook recording practices.

===FINDING 9===
LEAD: Payment-voucher activity in the sample follows recurring monthly and quarterly cycles, suggesting that payments may be concentrated at predictable points in the year. This pattern should be checked for administrative or financial-year-end bunching.
DETAIL: No comparable cycle was evident across fiscal years, whose totals ranged from 1,003 vouchers in 2023-24 to 1,985 in 2025-26. The analysis identifies repetition but not its cause, so reviews should compare the high-activity periods with fund releases, bill processing, work completion and data-entry dates.

===FINDING 11===
LEAD: Activity-linked expenditure is rising quarter by quarter in six of the nine sampled districts, but Bargarh, Koraput and Cuttack follow different trajectories. These three districts should be asked to explain whether their pattern reflects implementation timing or record-linking differences.
DETAIL: The increasing pattern was found in Khordha, Ganjam, Kandhamal, Sundargarh, Malkangiri and Rayagada. Across the sample, several of the highest quarters were January–March quarters, including Rs 1.99 crore in 2026-Q1 and Rs 1.92 crore in 2025-Q1; officials should check for year-end concentration and note that the Rs 0 recorded in 2020-Q2 and Q3 means no activity-linked expenditure was captured, not necessarily that no spending occurred.

===FINDING 16===
LEAD: Most cashbook measures—including payment and receipt amounts and voucher counts—repeat on a roughly annual cycle, while activity-linked expenditure repeats more frequently, about every three months. Sanctions do not follow either common pattern.
DETAIL: The annual cycle appears in total and average cashbook inflows and outflows, as well as payment and receipt counts. Sanction counts and amounts show different timing, so the next review should compare when sanctions are issued, when payments enter the cashbook and when expenditure is linked to activities; the pattern alone does not establish delay or irregularity.

===FINDING 20===
LEAD: The timing of activity-linked expenditure differs markedly across districts, indicating that a single statewide spending calendar may not describe the sampled GPs well. Sundargarh and Rayagada show much shorter cycles than the five districts following a three-year pattern.
DETAIL: Khordha, Bargarh, Ganjam, Koraput and Cuttack show a cycle repeating every 12 quarters, Sundargarh every six quarters and Rayagada every three; Kandhamal and Malkangiri show other patterns. Because the data cover only 24 quarters, the longer cycle is based on limited repetition and should be treated cautiously; districts should be asked whether fund-release schedules, work types, seasonal conditions or recording practices explain the differences.

===FINDING 23===
LEAD: Receipt-voucher recording follows recurring monthly and quarterly cycles, but annual receipt counts have not followed the same pattern. Officials should check whether inflow entries are being processed in periodic batches.
DETAIL: Annual receipt vouchers declined from 816 in 2020-21 to 555 in 2024-25, with 565 recorded in 2025-26, out of 3,911 across the sample. The detected cycles do not identify their cause, so high-entry periods should be compared with fund-release dates, bank credits and cashbook posting dates.

===FINDING 24===
LEAD: The number of sanctions in the sample has increased strongly, from 155 in 2020-21 to 485 in 2025-26. The rise is clear at quarterly and annual levels, although month-to-month sanctioning follows a different pattern.
DETAIL: A total of 2,040 sanctions were recorded, with 404 in 2024-25 and 485 in 2025-26. Officials should check whether the increase represents more approved works, smaller sanctions, changes in schemes or improved entry of sanction records, and whether monthly clustering is creating downstream pressure on implementation.

===FINDING 26===
LEAD: Activity-linked expenditure is rising quarter by quarter in nine of the 16 sampled blocks, while seven blocks show different patterns. The exceptions should be reviewed for stalled growth, irregular timing or differences in linking payments to plans.
DETAIL: The increasing blocks are Bhubaneswar, Khallikote, Khajuripada, Lahunipara, Kalimela, Kalyansingpur, Balisankara, Laxmipur and Sheragada. Barpali, Bheden, Rangeilunda, Boipariguda, Baranga, Tangi Choudwar and Attabira differ; officials should compare their quarterly records with sanctions, completed works and cashbook payments before drawing conclusions about performance.

===FINDING 27===
LEAD: Ganjam’s cashbook activity changed sharply around August 2020, while activity-linked expenditure and sanctions shifted later, in October–November 2020. The staggered change warrants a check for changes in operations, data entry or payment-to-activity linking.
DETAIL: Payment and receipt amounts, voucher counts and their per-GP monthly averages shifted in August; sanction counts and amounts shifted in October, and activity-linked expenditure in November. As these dates fall near the beginning of the dataset, the result may reflect system uptake or incomplete early records rather than a real operational change, so Ganjam should verify data completeness and any process changes during that period.

===FINDING 28===
LEAD: In 2025-26, Ganjam led the sampled districts on six of nine measures, including total inflows, outflows, activity-linked expenditure and sanctions. Its lead does not extend to payment-voucher count or both per-GP monthly averages, so scale and intensity should be assessed separately.
DETAIL: Ganjam accounted for 26.1% of the 1,985 payment vouchers, behind Khordha’s 28.6%, and its average monthly payment per GP was Rs 7.78 lakh. Officials should examine whether Ganjam’s high totals arise from the number of GPs represented, larger transactions or higher implementation, rather than treating the district ranking alone as a performance result.

===FINDING 29===
LEAD: Within 2020-21, sanctioned amounts increased across months and quarters, with Rs 2.48 crore sanctioned in total. No conclusion about an annual trend is possible because only that one fiscal year is included in this finding.
DETAIL: The within-year increase may indicate a ramp-up in sanctioning during 2020-21, but it could also reflect the timing of programme commencement or record entry. Reviewers should examine the monthly sanction dates and compare them with approvals and fund releases before interpreting the rise as improved performance.

===FINDING 30===
LEAD: Bhubaneswar’s activity-linked expenditure shows an overall increase at monthly, quarterly and annual levels, reaching Rs 1.01 crore in 2025-26. This is up from no recorded activity-linked expenditure in 2020-21.
DETAIL: Bhubaneswar recorded Rs 3.26 crore across the six years, although the annual path included a fall from Rs 74.21 lakh in 2022-23 to Rs 30.60 lakh in 2023-24 before recovering. Officials should verify whether the initial zero and subsequent growth reflect actual implementation, improved linking of cashbook payments to activities or both.

===FINDING 31===
LEAD: Bargarh shows a clear split: Bheden leads on cashbook payments, receipts and voucher activity, while Barpali leads on sanctions and activity-linked expenditure. This mismatch is worth reconciling against planned works and payment-linking practices.
DETAIL: Bheden accounted for 57.2% of the 1,546 payment vouchers in Bargarh and averaged Rs 8.74 lakh in monthly payments per GP, compared with Rs 2.28 lakh in Barpali and Rs 2.22 lakh in Attabira. Officials should check whether Bheden’s cashbook volume includes payments not linked to planned activities, and whether Barpali’s higher sanctions are translating into expenditure and completed works.

===FINDING 32===
LEAD: During 2024-25, the typical monthly payment per GP increased across months and quarters, suggesting higher outflows later in the year. The annual average was Rs 3.99 lakh per GP-month.
DETAIL: The annual figure is based on 240 GP-month records, but only one fiscal year is in scope, so no year-on-year trend can be inferred. Officials should check whether the within-year rise reflects normal implementation timing or a concentration of payments toward year-end, and compare it with work completion and voucher dates.
